speechtext: Mr. D. M. KENNEDY (West Edmonton) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 41, to amend the Railway Act, 1919.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919, AMENDMENT

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT, 1919, AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This is a bill to amend sections 314 and 318 of the Railway Act, 1919. Section 314, which deals with equal tolls to be charged by the railways, contains two qualifying phrases which permit of all sorts of inequalities. It is proposed to amend this section by striking out these two qualifying phrases. The first phrase, in the first and second lines, reads "under substantially similar circumstances and conditions," and the second phrase, in the fourth line, reads "passing over the same line or route." Section 318 deals with facilities to be afforded for the movement of grain from the western provinces to Lake Superior terminals and destinations east. It is proposed to amend this section so as to make it apply to destinations on the Pacific coast also.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first
time.

speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman has exhausted his right to put questions on the Orders of the Day.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: With all deference, Mr. Speaker, I must object to that ruling. There is no exhaustion of the right to put questions on the Orders of the Day; there is no limit of this right on the part of any single member of parliament.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: There are .pages of precedents in Bourinot and May respecting the right of members to put questions to the government and offer personal explanations before the Orders of the Day are called. The privilege is one which must not be unduly encroached upon. Questions put to the ministry must be to the point and must be brief. One member may put a question, but if he submits a series of questions it would block the business of the House. I think I am very liberal and generous with regard to the putting of such questions, but I must not be over-generous.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: I do not want to be understood as saying that there is not a strict limitation as to the character of questions -that can be put. What I wish to say is, that there is no limitation as to the number of questions that can be put by any individual member so long as they come within the circumference of interrogations of a proper character.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: In cases of great urgency it has been the practice to allow questions to be put on the Orders of the Day, but it is a salutary and customary rule to follow-in justice to the government and in order that questions shall be of a proper character and that they shall be properly answered-that interrogations go on the order paper. That has been the practice for years.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
With regard to the practice of putting oral questions, without any notice given, let me call the attention of hon. members to paragraph 311 under rule 31 in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms:
When the Orders of the Day are called by the Speaker and before they are read by the clerk assistant, it is the practice sanctioned by usage but not by any positive rule, for members to make personal explanations or ask questions of the government, in reference to an inaccurate report of their speeches in the official records, or in the newspapers : or in denial of certain charges made against them in the public prints; or in reference to certain remarks which had been misunderstood on a previous occasion, and which they had not before had an 
opportunity of explaining; or in respect to delay in obtaining returns or to the incompleteness of certain returns brought down under the order of the House; or relative to the state of public business, or other matters of public interest. But these remarks should be brief, as they are only tolerated, there being no question before the Chair when they are made, and no discussion should be allowed when a minister lies replied to a question, nor after a member has mad-a personal explanation. In asking a question, a member must not attack the conduct of the government. If a member wishes to make personal explanations in reference to the remarks which have fallen from another member the latter ought to be in his place.
In the present ease, there is nothing before the Chair as the Orders of the Day are called, and. therefore, if by tolerance the Chair allows a member to put some question to the government, and even to repeat the question, it should be strictly confined to public business. Besides, private members should confine themselves to one question and not multiply them; otherwise the business of the House will be blocked. I hope, however, that hon. members will not think I am lecturing them, because it is for the proper carrying out of the business of the House that, I make these remarks.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: I do not know that the present case is so important that it should be pressed, but the principle is important. I venture to say it has never been ruled that any private member must limit himself to one question on the Orders of the Day. I know it is a matter of tolerance, and I am quite in conformity with the statement of the principle that there should be brevity in asking the question, that it should be of some immediate import, and that upon the reply being given discussion cannot follow. But I really must dissent, and dissent emphatically, from a ruling which says that no member can ask two questions on the Orders of the Day, provided they come within the well known rules . of parliament, as set forth in the authorities.

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, February 28th, consideration of the proposed motion of Mr. Good with respect to racetrack betting.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subtopic: RACE-TRACK BETTING MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to continue this debate on the important resolution that we heard discussed yesterday, I wish to state at the outset my position in regard to the resolution. I am unreservedly in favour of the resolution.
I do not take that position because of' any unfortunate circumstances, as far as I am personally concerned, in the past, in connection with gambling because my experience along the lines of gambling have been very limited indeed. I can recall one occasion being in our neighbouring country to the south of the international line, in one of their prosperous cities, and coming across what was called the nickel slot machine. Being young and foolish, I wras induced to drop a nickel in the customary place, and I was very much surprised to see eleven nickels roll out. I do not know whether that was gambling or not, but my natural national instinct possessed me at that time, and I put the money in my pocket and went away. Outside of that experience, about the only other chance experience that I have undertaken ivas when, in the fall of 1921, I dared to presume to attempt to make a living in parliamentary life, and I venture to state that if certain hon. members in this corner of the House have their way I may not be even able to make a living in this line. I had hoped when this resolution was proposed that it' would be carried unanimously and would not occasion very much debate, but I recall that yesterday afternoon there were very many cries of "lost," and two hon. members of the House made lengthy arguments in opposition to the tenor of the resolution.
The hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rin-fret) brought out some statements in connection with this resolution. His statements did not seem very weighty, but nevertheless they "were made. One was that the tendency of the resolution was to introduce a new offence, that of race betting. He meant by that,. I presume, that if we make the business of gambling on a race-track illegal, we would encourage gambling and there would be more
of it. That is what one might call a "catch" statement. It is similar to the statement we so often hear that closing the public bars has led to more drinking than if they were left open, and it is just as erroneous and without any more foundation than that statement. The hon. member also stated that if we cannot have betting, we cannot have horse racing.
I wonder why. Is it necessary to have a large number of Americans of the loose and immoral type of both sexes come across to Canada and go from one race-track to another in order to keep up horse racing? Is this the kind of patronage that good Canadians want in order to develop the horse-breeding industry? I should think surely not. The hon. member stated that he does not believe in prohibition, and that he would like to prohibit prohibition itself. I wonder if he was sincere in that statement. What about murder? What about stealing? What about pulling a gun on a man? Some few weeks ago we had in this city a case of one man pulling a gun on another man and shooting him dead. I presume that the hon. member would hot interfere with personal liberty and prohibit a man from pulling a gun on another.
We listened yesterday to the argument, or some statements at least, of the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie). He stated that in Great Britain he saw some of the finest looking people he ever saw in his life, and they were betting. The inference we draw from that is that betting improves the looks of a person. I presume the hon. member has bet a good deal in his time, and that is why he looks so much better than the rest of us. The same hon. member stated that it was possible to get a bet on the races in California or New Orleans in certain parts of Ottawa to-day, meaning yesterday. I should like to ask-should we establish the old bar and saloon system because it is possible, through some bootlegger, to get some home-brew to-day? I think not, and I think if the people of Canada had the say, a large majority would unquestionably say, no. The same hon. member stated that British settlers should be given the privilege of a few things to which they are accustomed. I fancy a large number of our best British immigrants are coming out to Canada in order to get away from those veiy things, saloons, barrooms, betting and gambling, which are all too prevalent in their home land.
Possibly none of us here to-day can fail to understand that there are certain good things in this world, and that there is a source from which all good things come. We have our different lines of industry; we have our differ-

ent industrial concerns, such as lumbering, manufacturing, agricultural pursuits, fishing, shipbuilding and such like. We have our labouring class of people, the labour that they perform, and the blessings that accompany honest toil. We also have throughout our land our different church organizations and all that they stand for. We have our different social reform societies, and we have our elaborate school system-our public schools, high schools or collegiates, and our colleges or universities; and we need not elaborate on what they stand for and the beneficial influence that they have on our national life. These different organizations or institutions tend to develop the individual. They tend to develop his personality, to improve and develop his intellect, his judgment, his reason; and they also, together, through the influences they exert, tend to promote, we might say, those finer qualities of citizenship, kindness and charitable feelings for other people. I think we are all agreed that from the source of good, emanate those good influences that tend to upbuild our citizenship, to strengthen the individual and to produce better characters in our land. One might think of this as a good tree which cannot bring forth corrupt fruit.
On the other side of the picture, we, I think, are quite able to understand that we also have certain evil conditions in this land as well as in other countries, and that these evil conditions emanate from an evil source. It is easy for us to understand what is meant by social upheavals, by distrust amongst members of society, by lack of confidence of man in man, or one member of society in another member of society, leading to social unrest and instability, it may be of government. All these tendencies emanating from the evil source tend to pull down and to destroy personality in the-individual. They tend to lay aside reason, judgment, intelligence and willpower, and instead they develop and promote emotions and passions, so that we have following in this train, a long list of evil happenings, such as dishonest proceedings, cheating, embezzlement, forgery, debt, bankruptcy, and even suicide and murder. These all follow along the line of the evil channel, and this is equivalent to saying that an evil tree cannot bring forth good fruit.
We might ask the question, where does gambling come in? Does it come in under the shade of the good tree, or under the influence of the evil tree. A short definition of gambling might be "a stake upon chance for gaining without labour." I do not know whether my opinion as regards whether gambling is an evil or not, would be accepted as being of 
very much account; but I recall that some few weeks ago we had the annual meeting of the Social Service Council of Canada in this city, and the venerable president, the Rev. Dean Tucker, made a statement which was very significant. He said that the three great evils in the world were impurity, intemperance and gambling. He classified gambling as one of the great evils in the world to-day. In addition to his statement I would produce some evidence taken from the journals of the House of Commons, 1909-10, Vol. 45, on race-track gambling, given at the time the Miller bill was under consideration. Certain questions are asked of Mr. Walter Duncan, who had been inspector of detectives for the city of Toronto for something like twenty-two years. He was asked:
Would you classify whiskey and gambling as the two chief sources of the troubles that your department has to cope with?
A. Yes.
Q. Gambling generally?
A. Gambling generally.
Q. Including horse-racing gambling, whether it is gambling off the track or on the track, and every other kind?
A. Every other kind.
I would also quote a statement that appears in the same volume by Inspector Archibald, who was chief inspector of the Toronto police force for more than forty years. In his experience something like 60,000 cases had come before him for consideration, and the question was asked him:
Coming back to your own department of work, of these 60,000 cases that came to you by way of complaint, what was the principal cause at the bottom of the trouble in the majority of the cases?
A. I have no doubt that directly or indirectly the inordinate use of liquor was the cause in the majority of cases.
Then another question was asked him:
Q. What would figure1 second, where would gambling
come in?
A. Gambling came up pretty close to the liquor business. I think perhaps it would be second in order, but not nearly to the same extent as the liquor.
Let me quote from the same source a statement reputed to have been made by Mr. A. H. Clarke, a representative of South Essex, in this House. He made this statement on 1st May, 1905, and it can be found in Hansard of that year, at page 5138:
I happen to reside in a city where we have horse races, where there is a great deal of betting, and I can say there is no greater curse to the community than this race-track. The horse races are incidental; the gambling and betting is the main issue. I know nothing that has ruined more young men in that vicinity than this very race track. It has been my experience to have jfo prosecute several young men who

Race-track Betting
were in trusted positions, but who had squandered the money of their employers, all traceable to this race track.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the evidence of these gentlemen is perhaps more convincing than any statement or argument that I might put forth here to-day. While I have no experience of gambling on race-tracks, I have some knowledge of gambling conditions as they prevail in our prairie country. It might be presumed that the people out on the prairies ai'e so busy growing wheat and trying to get a market for it that they have nothing else to think of. Well, that might be true with the majority of landowners. But we have a number of young people who come into that country, more especially in harvest and threshing time, and who earn good wages and then drift into the small towns and villages on towards the fall of the year. And, sad to say, they are relieved of their hard earnings in a very short time. It some cases it takes but one or two nights for them to lose some S200 or $300 of hard-earned money. Now, it might be wondered why this is not stopped. Well, it seems that there is a certain provision in the Criminal Code that makes it possible for this business to be carried on. In section 226A we have it stated that a common gaming-house is a house, room, or place kept by	any	person for gain.
Then further on, in "B," (1A) it says that a gaming-house is a place where the whole or any portion of the stakes or bets is either directly or indirectly paid to the person keeping such house, room or place. There is just the little snag in this section of the Criminal Code which we find it difficult to get around. And it is of my own knowledge that I speak. In the town where I live we have known gambling to go on in one of our hotels for some time, but it was impossible to get any convicting evidence because it was necessary to prove that a rake-off from the game was going to the proprietor of the house. Finally, some two years ago, one of the gamblers had a quarrel with the proprietor of the house and informed on him and he was summoned and fined. But to-day in that western town, I venture to state gambling is going on, not only in this same hotel, but in a couple of Chinese restaurants. You might wonder whether it is possible for gambling to go on in a public place of that kind, and perhaps the question occurs, what is wrong? It seems to me that gambling carried on in a hotel or in a restaurant, in a poolroom, in a park, or on a race-track should all be included under the same head and be prohibited by Dominion statute.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to state my interpretation of the resolution offered by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) and to give my opinion of what would be its effect if adopted.
To understand the resolution we must go back to 1906 and review the law then in force governing horse-racing. Section 235 of the Criminal Code, which the hon. member now proposes to amend, as it stood in the Revised Statutes of 1906, made certain prohibitions regarding betting, book-making, poolselling, and the becoming custodian or depository of money, property, or other valuable thing staked, wagered or pledged. By subsection 2 of the same section it was provided :
The provision of this section shall not extend to any person by reason of his becoming the custodian or depository of any money, property or valuable thing staked, to be paid to the winner of any lawful race, sport, game or exercise, or to the owner of any horse engaged in any lawful race, or to bets between individuals or made on the race course of an incorporated association during the actual progress of a race meeting.
In other words, every citizen was allowed to be the custodian or depository of money or valuable property to be paid to the winner of a lawful race, sport, game or exercise, or to the owner of a horse engaged in a lawful race; and betting was allowed between individuals without any restrictions as to their number or the amount of money wagered, so long as such betting took place

on the race course of an incorporated association.
In 1910 the law was amended by the enactment of the provisions contained in what was afterwards known as the Miller Bill. Section 235 was amended in its first subsection by adding to the number of the prohibitions, and the second subsection was amended by adding to the exceptions. That is to say, all the exceptions in the law of 1906 were maintained and additional exceptions were enacted. Among those exceptions we find that betting was allowed on the race courses of incorporated associations during race meetings; that individuals were allowed to conduct book-making, etc., on such racecourses. There were also stipulations as to the number of race meetings to be held in each calendar year, the interval between such meetings, and their duration. In 1912 the same article was amended de novo, to provide that all these exceptions that I have just mentioned should be restricted to associations incorporated in any manner before the 20th day of March, 1912, and to all other associations incorporated by the federal parliament or by the legislatures after that date. In 1920, after that royal commission investigation which has been mentioned during the course of this debate had been held, another amendment was made to that same article 235. Section 2 of article 235 was amended as to running races by continuing the same exceptions that I have already mentioned, and making an exception as to betting, which was to be limited to the pari-mutuel. Provisions were made to put into force that new system and giving the Minister of Agriculture supervisory control of the administration of that act. We had last year some amendments of minor importance to article 235.
The resolution offered by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) would involve the following changes in the law: First, the abolition of all special privileges now existing with regard to race-track betting for running races, pari-mutuels included; secondly, change the present exception of a private bet between individuals not engaged in any way in the business of betting to a private bet between not more than ten individuals not engaged in the betting business; and thirdly, remove the exception in favour of a stake to be paid to the owner of any horse engaged in any lawful race.
I have given you, Mr. Speaker, the law as we have it to-day with regard to horseracing; I have given you the changes which the resolution of the hon. member would bring

Race-track Betting
about if it was adopted. Are we ready in. this country to vote for what I would call such radical changes? Is there at this present moment any agitation in Canady which would justify such a change? I have not heard of any from the Maritime provinces; I do not know of any in the province of Quebec; I have not heard of any from British Columbia or the other western provinces. We have heard some from the province of Ontario. Yesterday the hon. member for Brant gave us some of the utterances delivered by the Attorney General for Ontario, the Hon. Mr. Raney. He quoted the Hon. Mr. Raney as his main authority, I would say, to justify his resolution. I am not sure that I shall surprise the hon. member for Brant, but I may tell him this, that the Hon. Mr. Raney has never asked for any such amendment as the amendment my hon. friend now proposes to this House.
I have had the pleasure of corresponding with the Hon. Mr. Raney on this very subject for a month or so, and not later than yesterday I had the honour to receive in my office the deputy Attorney General for Ontario, who came to me with the Crown Prosecutor for Toronto, at the special request of the Attorney General of Ontario, to ask me to submit to the consideration of the hon. members of this House certain amendments to article 235. They never asked, Mr. Raney never asked, that we should repeal section 2 of article 235, as the hon. member for Brant now proposes.
I will read to the House the amendment suggested by the Attorney General for Ontario and by the Crown Prosecutor for Toronto. Suggested amendement to section 235 of the criminal
code as enacted by section 3 of (1910) 9-10 Ed. VII,

(f) Advertises, prints, publishes, exhibits, posts up, sells or supplies, or offers to sell or supply (i) other than on the premises of an association lawfully conducting race meetings in Canada, and during the actual progress of a race meeting thereon, any tips, selections, odds, winning money prices, pari-mutuel payments, or any similar intelligence with respect to or applicable to any horse race, whether such race be held within or without the Dominion of Canada, and whether at the time of advertising, printing, publishing, exhibiting, posting up or applying such news or information such race has or has not taken place; (ii) any information intended to assist in or intended for use in connection with book-making, pool-selling, betting or wagering upon any fight, game, sport or race, other than a horse race whether at the time of advertising, printing, publishing, exhibiting, posting up or supplying such news or information, such fight, game, sport or race has or has not taken place.
This is to do away with the abuse against which we are receiving complaints. There is unquestionably ground for complaint about betting and book-making on races in the United States, where races are prohibited, and where they flourish more than ever.

Mr. Speaker, I have followed with great interest the debate which has taken place on this resolution. I have heard some very strong arguments in support of the prohibition which is advocated, but I have not heard any arguments which were not advanced in 1906, in 1910, in 1912 and in 1920. In a word, there was nothing new in any of the speeches delivered during the present debate which I followed very attentively. I repeat, that to my mind there is actually no agitation in this country for so radical a change as the one which is proposed by the hon. member for Brant. Why should we not be satisfied with amending our criminal code in accordance with the suggestions which have come to us, the only sugestions which have come to us officially from the Ontario government? I -am prepared to recommend ter my colleagues that we should make a government measure of the substance of the amendments which I have just read to the House and with this, it seems to me, hon. gentlemen should be *satisfied, leaving to experience the legislation of 1920 which was passed after mature consideration.
If the hon. member who has submitted this resolution intends to press it to a vote, and if we are at this session, or some other session, to consider legislation which will make legal the new prohibition which is now advocated, I would suggest, for my part, that we at least make it optional for the provinces to accept that prohibition if they so desire, or to refuse it if such is their wish. We have already had experience in another field on a question which has given some very good results; and I think that for the good

of the country, before imposing the change in whose behalf the resolution has been offered, we should leave it to the provinces to decide.
Mr. Speaker, we already have enough causes of difference in this country. Though that be the case I am not alarmed at them. I believe in the future of my country, and I know that ultimately all these differences will pass one after another. Nevertheless I deem it to be the duty of every man of good will in Canada to do nothing that will add to the number of our differences, and it is in that spirit that I would ask hon. members who believe in this new prohibition-and I respect their opinion-not to consider it important enough to impose it on the Dominion against the will of a large proportion, if not the majority, of its population.

speechtext:
In rising to continue this debate let me assure the House that I do not intend to speak at any great length. I shall devote my remarks mainly to the ethical feature of the question that is now before us, but I shall allude to certain other aspects as well.
In the first place I want to make it very clear that in principle I am absolutely opposed to betting, and in the remarks which I shall offer I propose to hew to the line. I desire to be frank and explicit in my expressions of opinion; I believe in calling a spade a spade. The resolution has been very ably supported by the hon. member who introduced it, and by other members as well. Very substantial arguments and a mass of figures have been advanced in its favour. I do not wish to go over ground which has been so'sthoroughly well covered, but I would like to refer to points which have been raised by opponents of the resolution. One hon. member asked who were behind this motion, who were its promoters. In answer to that question I can produce the sworn statement of a gentleman who gave evidence before the Rutherford Commission as to who are behind the movement now and who were supporting it at that particular time. I will quote the statements of Mr. W. E. Raney, K.C., who appeared before that commission:
Mr. W. E. Raney, K.C., appeared for the Social Service Council of Canada, which he stated was a federation comprising a considerable number of units, including,-the Church of England in Canada, the Methodist Church in Canada, the Presbyterian Church in Canada, the Baptist Church in Canada, the Congregational Church in Canada, the Salvation Army, the Dominion Grange and Fanners' Association, The Dominion Women's. Christian Temperance Union, the National Council of the Young Men's Christian Association, the Canadian Council of Agriculture and some dozen other organizations, He stated that the Social
[Sir Lomer Gouin.I
Service Council did not oppose racing either as a sport or as a test of the metal or endurance of the thoroughbred horse, but that it took objection to the exception made by the criminal code which legalized race-track betting.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that is the force that is behind this movement, so far as I can -understand. If that be true, the force that is behind the resolution that has been presented to this House by the hon. member for Brant, it is no mean element of the people of the Dominion of Canada. I want to refer to a statement made, I think, by the hon. ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) in regard to the necessity of this movement for keeping up the race-courses in this country. I quote from Hansard of yesterday:
We find that you cannot get the proper number of horses for the purposes of a really good meeting on this side of the line in the face of the competition, unless you are able to attract them by large purses.
I do not know anything personally in regard to the amount of money the racing clubs give in the way of purses to encourage race-track enterprises in the Dominion, but I am going to quote again from the latter part of Dr. Rutherford's report, where he is referring to this aspect of the race-track enterprise. He says:
While, as shown elsewhere in this report, certain racing associations have been reasonably generous in the giving of special purses for Canadian-bred horses at the regular race meeting others have not distinguished themselves in that respect. It is, however, apparent that, notwithstanding the large profits which have accrued, there has been but little inclination on the part of any of them, to offer direct financial assistance to the horsebreeding industry.
It has been presented very forcibly by some hon. members in opposition to this resolution, that racing is almost absolutely necessary, if I understood them aright, for keeping up thoroughbred horses in the Dominion of Canada. And yet we find that in summing up his report Dr. Rutherford does not give the race club organizations very much credit for giving of the money that they took in to any great extent by way of purses for the sake of encouraging this enterprise.
Yesterday hon. members referred to the necessity of having betting on race-tracks properly regulated. I quote again from the remarks of the ex-Minister of Agriculture yesterday, where he says:
Far better to apply a law and have people betting out in the open than to restrict betting and have it carried on illegally behind a curtain.
To my mind, we are casting a reflection on the integrity, the honesty and the fidelity of the people of this great Dominion, if we intimate in any way that, if the people can-

Race-track Betting
not bet under regulated conditions, they are going to bet illegally behind closed doors. I have more faith in the people of the country than to assent to that suggestion. True, there may be, and is, illegal betting, but we know that crime goes on in spite of regulation. We have stringent regulations in regard to murder, theft and in a great many other things, anl yet these crimes go on, and the men who are guilty of those crimes are guilty of breaking the law. If betting is an evil and injurious to the best interests of the people, regardless of where it is carried on, whether in the closed room or on the race-track, the proper way to deal with it is to pass a law prohibiting it, so that it will be easy for men to do right and hard for them to do wrong. My judgment is that laws are made for the purpose of making it hard for men to do wrong, and easy for them to dip right. Take the case of the rattlesnake. How are you going to regulate that animal? I think there is just one way to regulate that very treacherous and dangerous reptile, and that is by cutting off its head. I believe that is just as true in regard to any social evil or any evil that has a tendency to divert men or women from straight paths of virtue and truthfulness, honesty and uprightness. As honest, truthful and faithful citizens of any country, if we are going to regulate those evils, the better way is to outlaw them rather than to try to legalize them as something honourable and something to be desired.

speechtext:
In answer to the hon. member's question, I suppose there is a difference between regulation and amputation, but the way I would regulate a rattlesnake would be by amputation and the way I would regulate any evil in this country would be by amputation instead of regulation by law.' I would make it illegal.
Touching on the ethical side of this feature perhaps for a moment, what is gambling? Is it not the fact that people are trying to get something for nothing? A man goes into your stable and steals your horse. He goes there to get something for nothing, but he goes there breaking the law. A man puts his hand into your pocket and takes out your money. He is after something for nothing, he is trying to get your money without doing anything for it; but he is breaking the law. But when a man goes into the betting arena and takes part in betting, he is looking to get something from somebody else for nothing, without labouring for it. We hear a good deal sometimes about loafing on the job and not wanting to work for what we get and getting something for nothing; but to my mind, if there is in this country anything that is a means of getting something for nothing, it is the gambling method, and on that ground I am opposed to the betting system as carried on at the race-tracks.
I have under my hand some figures that I got from the report of Dr. Rutherford and from the exhibits in his office; but many of these figures were quoted yesterday by the hon. member (Mr. Good) who introduced this resolution, and therefore, I am not going to repeat them to-day. I want, however, to draw the attention of the House to the difference between the amount of money made by jockey clubs under the pari-mutuel system and what they had been making under the bookmaking system. In the Hamilton Jockey Club, in 1915, under bookmaking, they got $67,200. In 1916, under the parimutuel system, they got $182,825,50; that is for two meets. In 1917, for one meet which took place in that year, they got $173,429.05. In connection with the Windsor Jockey Club a similar jump took place. In 1914, under bookmaking, they got $81,150, under the parimutuel system, in 1915, they got $196,650.50; in 1916, $300,332,25; and in 1917, $159,779.94. Therefore, under this improved method, as I suppose it will be called, of pari-mutuel betting, the clubs receive a larger amount of money than they did under the old bookmaking system. The Niagara Racing Association at Fort Erie, in 1914, under bookmaking, got $64,344; in 1915, under the parimutuel system, they got $131,988.55. This represents an enormous sum of money, when we take into consideration the amount of money that goes out of the pockets of those who take part in the betting and goes onto the race track for the purpose of betting, for these amounts represent possibly only about 5 per cent of all the money that passes through these machines. A club is allowed to take, on a sliding scale, from seven to three per cent, so that possibly 5 per cent would be a fair estimate of the amount of money that a club receives in this way through the machine betting. I am opposed to the betting system for the reason that it is a system whereby men try to get something without working for it, or something for nothing.
I am also opposed to it, because, as we understand the matter, it is not in the best interest of the home. In connection with betting, an hon. member yesterday referred to
Rac.e-track Belting

the boys and girls. The boys and girls are the greatest asset this country has, and if we are going to safeguard them, we want to safeguard them to the very fullest extent by removing from them as far as possible every opportunity for indulging in anything that would have a tendency to draw them away. I believe gambling is a social evil. We believe in the social qualities of our human nature; we believe in social life; we believe in good healthy enjoyment, recreation and sport; we believe in all that kind of thing; but when these social enterprises go to the extent of being an evil, then it is time that we should rise up in opposition to them. My honest conviction is that betting, no matter how it is done, is a social evil, and we want to discourage it to the fullest extent in every regard, in every place and in every way, and to legislate so far as possible against that evil. There is something of the sensational in those gambling and betting affairs. There is something that appeals to the sensational feature in human nature.

Mr. Speaker, so much has been said both for and against the principles enunciated in this resolution that scarcely anything remains to be added. Therefore, beyond expressing my own attitude in the most unequivocal language, I have very little to say. I have watched from time to time with keen interest the attitude of parliament towards questions that are vitally important to our standards of citizenship or morality, and I have observed ' two entirely opposite schools of thought. One
Race-track Betting

seems to base its argument on the value of the dollar; the other on the value of citizenship. As I have always found myself sympathetic towards the latter I am obliged to support the resolution, although to my mind it may be a bit drastic.
Very full statistics have been presented during the course of this debate showing the profits of race-track gambling to those concerned in it-to the individual, to the company, and even to the province. Facts have also been adduced showing the baneful effects of race-track gambling upon our citizenship. I need not repeat the arguments based on these facts and figures, for they are before the minds of hon. gentlemen; I would only suggest that all social customs are judged by the effects they produce. It is not very difficult, therefore to estimate their value or the reverse. And in regard to race-track gambling, it may be safely said that its so-called benefits are mixed pretty generously with injustice and degeneracy.
I would be sorry indeed to have 5 p.m. Canadians get the impression that parliament is in any way indifferent to social questions of paramount importance. Of course, great caution must be taken in enacting restrictive legislation; extremes are to be avoided; but good statesmanship always avoids extremes. On the other hand, it is dangerous to yield to the much talked of principle of individual liberty of action. Our whole criminal code in many instances is based on the very sound maxim that such individual liberty of action is not always permissible, and may conceivably be decidedly dangerous to the community.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I humbly urge parliament to in some way put greater restrictions on this particular menace which threatens our very civilization; for no nation can rise above its standard of morality.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak to this resolution, but in view of the attitude of certain hon. members towards this very important national question, I must do my duty and at least declare my stand in regard to what I consider to be of the highest moral as well as economic importance.
Our young people have held out to them the prospect of getting rich quick through gambling-of winning something for which they give no equivalent. The very idea is demoralizing and brings in its train untold evils. Young men, yes, and young women too, are induced to risk their all on something which is purely chance. Gambling, I know, [Mr SexsmithJ
is latent in humanity, and those who make their living by this vicious practice are generally adepts in reading human nature. A very small beginning is sufficient to start one on the downward road, the game of chance being extremely fascinating, and it is not long before young men and women find their earnings too small to satisfy their cravings to wager on bigger and bigger chances. Unfortunately, too often this leads to their appropriating the funds of their employers, fully intending, of course, to replace the money in the near future, but the more they wager on these so-called sure things the more they lose. Then what? They abscond and too often they commit suicide. I know whereof I speak. I have in mind two valuable lives snuffed out- suicides from gambling losses. Therefore I cannot treat this matter as lightly as some hon. members on the other side of the House appear to do.
To me it is folly to talk of controlling such an evil. It cannot be controlled in all its ramifications. I think it is a serious matter indeed that we as a nation should countenance such a national evil by giving it legal sanction. The pari-mutuel business has been made unlawful in Great Britain, and those engaged in it are looked upon as rogues and vagabonds. In nearly all the states of the Union the practice is criminal, and those engaged in it have been driven hither and thither-mostly to Canada. Is this country, then, to become a haven of refuge for such characters, in whose train vices of all kinds follow? All commercial concerns know the baneful effect of betting upon their employees. A senior official of the Civil Service in this city is responsible for the statement that the Civil Service itself is honeycombed with betting. Now, that surely brings this evil pretty close home to every hon. member who cares anything for the uplift of our national character.
It is strange that some hon. members fail to realize the evils of race track gambling, and it is stranger still that public men can be found to uphold such a practice. Even if moral reasons fail to appeal, surely economic reasons should be considered when deciding our attitude in regard to this resolution. The Quebec Board of Trade on its own initiative passed a resolution asking for the suppression of this curse.

I wish to make a few remarks on this resolution before the vote is taken. I want to say at the outset that I am going to vote for the resolution. I ana going to do so_ for two particular reasons, and I hope without offence to those who think differently from me. It is largely I find, Mr. Speaker, a matter of how we have been brought up how we look upon questions such as this that we are discussing this afternoon. I have been brought up to look upon gambling, whether on the race-track or elsewhere, as fundamentally wrong, without one redeeming feature. Now then, Mr. Speaker, am I at my time of life going to make myself over again and think otherwise? I may add that my constituents-and I think I can speak for Saskatchewan as a whole-do not want to see legalized gambling on the racetracks established in that new land. It exists there to a small extent, but the time to nip these things is in the bud, not after large vested interests have been established when the plea ii? put up that the capital must receive from the state the protection that it is entitled to or supposed to be entitled to. Therefore I take the ground that now is the time to move in this matter as regards not only Saskatchewan but the entire prairie country.
The question has been raised as to whether there is any demand for this legislation or not, and attention has been drawn to the fact that there is no agitation for it in the Maritime provinces. Well, the records go to show that there are no gambling institutions of this nature in that part of Canada-no gambling associations, nor even a jockey club-therefore the people there are quite content the way the matter stands because it does not affect them. However, the records demonstrate that the practice is reasonably well established in the older provinces-in Ontario and Quebec

and also in British Columbia-but has only gained a slight footing in the new provinces on the prairie. I must say that it was a matter of considerable surprise to me, when I was first asked to assume the responsibility of administering the Department of Agriculture, to find that this to me doubtful practice of gambling was so unequally yoked with the ancient and respectable business of agriculture and that I was to administer the whole of it. Well, I have done so to the best of my ability, and if we are going to have gambling on race-tracks and its supervision is to be attached to some department, possibly the Department of Agriculture is the one to which it may more properly be allied. At the same time I feel somewhat embarrassed sometimes at having to administer this kind of business with which I am so unfamiliar.
Now what do the records show with respect to this matter? The government of Sir Robert Borden in 1917, in the midst of the war, took the ground that if Canada was to do her best in that war she could not afford to dissipate her resources to the extent she was then doing in the matter of gambling on race-tracks, and the practice was prohibited by order in council in that year. That prohibition, if my memory serves me, continued up to 1920. Why? Because the country could not afford to spend such a large amount of money in that kind of pleasure at that particular time. Well, Mr. Speaker, can we, from a purely material standpoint, afford to do it now? Is there any evidence that the situation is any better financially? Can we not employ all our money to better advantage than by dissipating it in this way

not only the money but the time and the thought of the people? And, to some extent, every man that makes easy money deters others from honest toil and honest labour and makes them dissatisfied. It does not matter how the easy money is made-whether in real estate speculation or in any other form of gambling or in any other way. It disturbs others who are engaged in earning their living by honest toil; and if for no other reason than that I would oppose this practice at this time. Because, if there is one idea more than another that we want to inculcate among our people it is the fact that there is only one way to make good in this world, only one way to make a living, and that is by honest industry faithfully and intelligently applied. Gambling weakens that idea and places its realization further away; there is no question about that. We can recall, during the time when real estate gambling was at its height, that when many men who were tilling the soil and making their living in a laborious way on the farm

As far as this government is concerned, it does not, because we do not get it. We have no interest in what any other government gets. The 5 per cent goes to help keep the association going and if you bet frequently enough, your money will all go that way. That 10 per cent is taken off each time it goes through the machine. There is no question about that. We cannot spend our money in these avenues and have it at the same time to spend on productive enterprises. That is the proposition from a straight business standpoint. I take the ground, knowing something of the difficulties of financing at the present time, that we can spend our money to better advantage than in the proposition I have outlined.
I have a few notes in my hand with respect to some remarks made yesterday by hon. members that were exceedingly painful to listen to. I refer to the excuses made for continuing the practice of gambling. I have no objection to the man who takes the ground "I want to gamble," but I have an objection to the man who wants to sugar coat the pill, and wants to justify it with a lot of camouflage on the ground that we are going to de-
TMr. Motherwell.]
velop the horse-breeding industry or something of that kind. I have not a word to say to those who want to gamble. They have just as much right to take that ground as I have to take the opposite ground, but I think no good thing comes out of gambling, taking the net results. I have read speeches about gambling, but I never expected to hear what we will have to call, by courtesy, arguments such as were advanced yesterday in justification of gambling. I have read of such things, but I thought a lot of these antediluvian ideas had gone to rest, because we have not heard of them for a number of years.
I should like to say a word in commendation of the report of Dr. Rutherford. I sat on a live stock commission myself with him. I know him to be an exceedingly capable man, and I think a just man, but I ask hon. members, is a man who is admittedly predisposed in favour of race-tracks, just as I am predisposed against them, a proper man to investigate a matter of this kind, or would either of us be fit men to deal with the question? I am quite sure if I were called on a jury in connection with this matter I would be challenged because my bringing up is against racetracks, and I would not be able to give a fair presentation of all sides of the case. I feel the same way with respect to Dr. Rutherford, but in saying that I am not saying anything disparaging of him. I am putting him in the same category as myself. I can remember quite well that in the province of Saskatchewan we thought we were making an advance when we authorized and recommended parimutuel machines at the exhibitions in that province, as a vast improvement on the old bookmaking method of betting, but the world moves in respect to these matters. I can remember when it was thought to be a great forward movement when we had local option in the liquor traffic. But Canada was not satisfied with that. She moved on, and is moving on now in reference to restrictions regarding gambling. What was all right ten years ago or even two years ago, with regard to pari-mutuels is not necessarily what Canada wants to-day. She wants further restriction. What we had ten years ago was sufficient for that day, but the public conscience of the country, so far as the West is concerned, is very much against commercialized gambling on the race-track.
The argument has been advanced: What is the use of legislating against gambling when you cannot carry your legislation into effect? If that argument is carried to its logical conclusion, it will apply to anything and every-

Race-track Betting
thing. What is the use of legislating against murder? What is the use of legislating against bawdy houses, or against any form of wrong doing, because forsooth, you cannot carry it into effect? If that argument prevailed we should open up the door as wide as a barn door, and throw all restraint to the winds. That is the logic of it. It is not an argument at all against it; if it is wrong, it is wrong, and it is our duty to legislate and to see that our law enforcement officers carry out the law as far as humanly possible, but if you preach the doctrine of legislative inaction on the ground that the law cannot be carried out, you simply cut the foundation from all law enforcement throughout Canada. We also cast disrespect upon ourselves and upon the laws of this country by whispering such an admission as that.
Then the doctrine was enunciated by my good friend whom I respect so highly, the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) -and it did pain me to hear him do it-that these investments should be protected. That is to say, this business having continued so long and great strings of horses, stables and race-tracks, having been established, it is not fair to those who have invested their money that their investment should be jeopardised by the prohibition of this practice. If we look back into history, we shall find that old cry, "Our craft is in danger," right from the time of Demetrius the silversmith onward. From his day to the present "Our craft is in danger" has been the cry in an attempt to justify the continuance of a practice that we know to be doubtful, if not actually wrong. Why, Demetrius would be at the job of making idols yet, if we took the ground that we must keep a man in his job regardless of the results. No, if a thing is wrong, it is wrong and the excuse or the reason advanced that we should protect money when invested in a wrong business will not hold water. I admit that my hon. friend made an exceedingly good presentation of an equally exceedingly bad case. I am prepared to compliment him to that extent; but just because he made such a good presentation, I feel it is my duty to show where the weak points of that case lie.
As regards my hon. friend's reference to Great Britain, I think the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) dealt sufficiently with that phase of the question. His covenanting disposition could not listen longer to the economic-almost religious-heresies that had been enunciated by my good friend the member for Victoria City. To associate the development of Great Britain, its civilisation,
its Christianity and the extent of its teaching of the Bible in any way with race-track gambling-I can remember the old Scotch covenanting people of the Maritime provinces and, indeed, throughout Canada looked upon it as almost sacrilege to mention these things in the same breath. I know quite well this was not meant so; but nevertheless it grated terribly on the ears of some of us, and I want to dissociate myself from any such arguments as that enunciated by my hon. friend, I am sure, quite unintentionally.. No, Great Britain is great in spite of these weaknesses of hers. That is the proper argument.
In regard to the question of horsebreeding,
I remember Dr. Rutherford advanced that argument, and on the face of it, it seems somewhat plausible until you inquire into it., I did not understand the hon. member for Victoria City to take the ground that thoroughbred animals could be used to improve the horsebreeding business generally throughout Canada. I think I am right in, that. But, at the same time, the argument has been used, in such a suggestive sort of way, that the thoroughbred has done so much good in the past. There is no question about the part which the thoroughbred has played during the last three or four hundred years in developing the various breeds in Great Britain. If I remember rightly, the thoroughbred was traced away back to Arabian horses, and it has come down to the present day. But certain strains have been introduced into many of the breeds of Great Britain and from there through Canada, just as the blood of the old longhorn cattle and even some of the black cattle has influenced the development of the present day shorthorn. All these have played their part in bringing down to us the various breeds of to-day. We can go into the plant world if you like. We know that what was called Abundance oats has a cross of wild oats in it to give it earlier maturity. But nobody is going to advocate the sowing of wild oats because there is a strain of wild oats in the variety know as Abundance. So, while the thoroughbred horse has played a great part in the past in developing the breeds of Great Britain, its work in that respect is done, and we cannot cross it with any of the various breeds of Canada without interfering with the right to registration. It can, of course, be used for building up remount stations; but how much attention do we desire to devote to that at this time? Hon. members know what the House felt like last year when we spoke of warlike expenditure, even in regard to ordinary defence or aircraft or the navy'. We cannot spent! much
Race-track Betting

money on remount stations. There is, however, a considerable sale for these animals, and because of that some attention is being paid to them; but so far as I can make out by the approximate estimates I have, the number of purebred stallions in Canada is about 9,000. Of that there are only 300 thoroughbreds, and we know that they are not used indiscriminately throughout Canada, but just in selected places where people want to raise saddle horses or hunters or remounts. That is the extent to which the thoroughbred can be utilised to develop the horsebreeding industry, so far as I understand the matter.

speechtext: As Minister of Agriculture does my hon. friend think that the abolition of horse-racing would interfere with the holding of agricultural fairs?

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subtopic: RACE-TRACK BETTING MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
That is a matter of education on the part of the people. I believe at the present time some agricultural fairs prohibit horse-racing entirely. Some take the ground that they must have a certain amount of recreation and pastime, we have what are called the midway and general platform sports. In the East I believe they feel that horse-racing is required in order to secure the maximum revenue. But if maximum revenue is the chief consideration, probably for a year or two the revenues would shrink by the abolition of horse-racing. You cannot have the thing both ways.
Let me continue with regard to the question of the effect upon breeding horses. I think I had almost concluded that point. I am willing to pay a tribute to the thoroughbred horse for what it has done to the various breeds in England and also in Canada, although its work in Canada has not been done directly, but has come down to us by importations in the past. But that work has been accomplished, and now it is confined only to the very restricted activities to which I have already referred.
I take the ground, when you strip this business of gambling from all the verbiage surrounding it, you have to defend it, in the last analysis, on its merits. There is no other way. I can recall the time when the fight against the liquor traffic was at its height. It used to be defended on the ground that it was associated with hotel accommodation, and people w'ould argue: "Well,' if we abolish the bar, we shall not have hotel accommodation." They had the two matters connected together and you could not get a straight [DOT] test vote as regards the abolition

of the bar. So, we have this question of race-track gambling surrounded with a halo oi glory inherited from the performances of the thoroughbred in former ages and people point to the accomplishments of the past as a justification for the continuance of racetrack gambling. In my time I have seen horse races where there was no gambling. Surely, we do not appreciate the beauty and glory of the horse, if we take the ground that there will be no racing if the gambling feature is taken away. That is tantamount to making the statement that if any other domestic animal you could think of were put on a race-track, as long as you could bet on it, the business would be just as successful as if the racing were done by horses. I take exception to that. There is no other domestic animal known that creates admiration to such an extent as the horse. We have found as a matter of fact, from experience, that horse-racing can be and has been developed to a very considerable extent without the supplemental aid of commercial betting.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY

Will the minister mention
some of the tracks where such unaided racing has been carried on successfully from year to year?

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY

speechtext:
The race-tracks did not try to carry on under that condition; they simply suspended their operations. It is a pretty difficult matter to make comparisons in this connection. The race-track people, when the order in council was passed in 1917, took it as an intimation from parliament that they were required to stop the whole business, and they did stop. I think they felt that the conscience of the country was against not only the expense involved but the business itself at that particular juncture in our history.
I now come to the last note I took on the subject, and that is the suggestion of the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin) with which I entirely agree, namely, that if we are to have further prohibition with respect to race-track gambling as well as to every other form of gambling-and, mark ycu, we have gone out of our way to legalize gambling on race-tracks while it is prohibited in other directions-then we should adopt it on a provincial basis. I want to say frankly that while I feel strongly on the question myself I should not feel justified in taking the attitude in the West that we should impose our will, even if we could, on the old established institutions of the eastern provinces; nor should I like to see the older provinces impose their views on the newer provinces that know very little about

Race-track Betting
the business but feel that it would lead to disastrous results. Last year we adopted that principle of tolerance with respect to the abolition of export houses in the seven dry provinces of Canada, and it went through the House with almost unanimous consent. There was no vote upon it, although there was some discussion. The right to deal with the export houses was conceded to the seven dry provinces and they can exercise that right. One province has taken advantage of it and another province, Alberta, is on the point of doing so. It seems to me that there is an avenue of solution whereby we can all get our own way provincially. And this principle can be worked out more satisfactorily i'i connection with race-track gambling than it can as applied to the export houses. The baneful effects of the liquor business can be felt all over the country, through some extraordinary process, notwithstanding the law. But with regard to race-meetings it is confined largely to the particular locality. I know there is a system to which my hon. friends refer, whereby, if you look around, you can get a bet in Ottawa, say, on a racemeeting in Kentucky. If that is so, and I have no doubt it is, it can be legislated against. But the point I wish to make is that although we feel strongly on this question, I am sure my hon. friends to my right would not wish to impose their modern view's upon us with respect to race-track gambling, nor would we impose our old-fashioned views upon them. That is reciprocity, and w'e all believe in that principle. In the multitude of counsellors, we are told, there is wisdom; and there is no reason why this solution should not be invoked as successfully in this matter as it was in the other case last year. In the meantime I shall vote for the resolution.

speechtext:
I rise to support the resolution moved by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good). The matter has been pretty well debated and I think the debate has been largely onesided. There are one or two comments which have been made to which I might reply for the benefit of those who are opposed to the resolution. Some hon. gentlemen opposite claim the moral right to do as they please in this matter, and I feel that they have a moral right to their views so long as they do not interfere with the liberties of other people. Our friends opposite sometimes accuse us of wishing to prohibit other people from doing what they want to do. On the other hand, we as farmers do not want to be injured in any way by men in the racing business. I am something like the Minister
of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell); while T have not suffered much from the evil influences of gambling, I would not want to see my sons buy fine horses and embark on the betting business or any other form of gambling. I do not think there is a banker in this country who wants to see one of his clerks engaged in race-track gambling, and undoubtedly that is the position of every other employer. The same thing might be said in regard to the liquor question. I believe that there is a certain amount of sincerity on the part of those who say that they have the right to a moderate use of liquor. But I do not think that a man has any right, while under the influence of liquor, to drive into Ottawa at the rate of thirty miles an hour regardless of whom he hurts. When he does so he interferes with the rights of other people and we have a right to legislate in the interests of the community at large. I happen to have been sent to parliament by a fairly representative body of people, and I should not be true to their wishes if I did not raise my voice in support of this resolution. I do not wish to detain the House on the question now, Mr. Speaker, and although there are several arguments which I might advance in support of it, as the subject has been fairly well covered, I shall not delay the progress of the House by any consideration of them.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subtopic: RACE-TRACK BETTING MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, stripped of its legal verbiage, what does this resolution proposed by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) ask for? Not that racing be stopped-racing, free from gambling, is a good, clean, inspiring, healthful sport. Not that private betting be interfered with-it cannot be legislated out of business; moral suasion alone must be relied on to do that. But as Britishers who love justice and fair play we ask that the business of betting on race-tracks be constituted a crime, as the business of betting off race-tracks is now and ever has been both in Canada and England constituted a crime; and that the pari-mutuel be prohibited as have the book-makers and the pool-sellers.
Before 1910 race-track betting was intended and supposed to be unlawful, and book-makers and pool-sellers were prosecuted. Some doubt, however, having been cast upon the validity of the law, in 1910 Mr. H. H. Miller, then representing South Grey, introduced into this House a bill to remedy some of the evils
Race-track Betting

of race-track gambling. The bill was referred to a select committee of the House, and after taking very exhaustive evidence from those opposed to and those in favour of race-track gambling, the committee recommended to the House the acceptance of the Miller Bill. The bill was debated for over two days, and was defeated by the narrow majority of one vote, there being seventy-eight in favour and seventy-seven against. Thereupon the business of betting by book-making, pool-selling and pari-mutuel received legal sanction, but racing meets were limited to fourteen days.
What happened? Racing meets rapidly multiplied; and the law being defective in prohibiting publication of betting odds and racing tips a general carnival of racing and an orgy of betting followed. So bad had conditions become that in 1917, during a critical period of the war, the government of the day, by virtue of the War Measures Act, and in the interests of economy, national welfare and morale, passed an order in council suppressing race-track betting until the close of the war. As a result racing was suspended, and the number of prosecutions against illegal betting houses rapidly declined.
In 1920 this order in council was rescinded and the government appointed a commission under the chairmanship of Dr. J. G. Rutherford to investigate race-track gambling. After a thorough and careful investigation this commission recommended that instead of suppressing race-track gambling the following restrictions be imposed, namely; that no bookmaking nor pool-selling be allowed; that parimutuels only be permitted; that a lower percentage of rake-off be allowed to jockey clubs; and that race-tracks be under the supervision of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The government of the day incorporated these recommendations into a bill which became law in October, 1920. The effectiveness of this legislation can be judged by the returns for 1921, the first year of its operation. The amounts wagered on the race-tracks of Ontario during the first half of the year 1917 up to August 1, when the order in council came into force, was $12,500,000. During the year 1921, under effective restriction, the amoimt wagered in Ontario had grown to the enormous sum of $56,778,596; in Quebec to $10,852,000, and for the rest of Canada about $10,000,000; or a total of something like $75,000,000. With this increase in legalized race-track betting, we find the prosecutions for illegal betting keeping pace. In the year 1919, under restrictions, we find that prosecutions for illegal betting had fallen to the small total of five. In the . year 1920, after this order was annulled, the number had increased to 26, and

during the year 1921, under effective restriction, the number of prosecutions for keeping of illegal betting houses had increased to the number of 55. No stronger argument is needed to refute the assertion that the legalizing of race-track gambling under government regulation would do away with illegal betting, or that the suppression of legalized racetrack gambling would drive people to the pool rooms and the betting houses to satisfy their speculative desires.
The debate, Mr. Speaker, we believe hinges very largely on the question as to whether the suppression of race-track gambling or effective restriction will best advance the national welfare. Some hon. members are very strong in their views as to the value of effective restriction and the evils of suppression or prohibition. I was somewhat amused to hear the arguments of my hon. friend from Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie) in this connection. If I remember correctly, in the province from which he comes they have a very live race problem, of a somewhat different nature. Only a few days ago a debate was begun in this House in support of a bill to better regulate oriental immigration. I think hon. meiri-bers will also remember the debate last session on a similar question, when the members from British Columbia cast all party affiliations to the winds and were a unit in demanding absolute exclusion of the oriental. Advancing by way of argument the international difficulties present, a member of the govern-' ment brought in an amendment substituting the words "effective restriction" for the word "exclusion". I believe that every hon. member from British Columbia, no matter where he sits in this House, voted against that amendment. The hon. member for Victoria City on that occasion asked: why do we hold out so strongly for the word "exclusion"? Simply because, he said, restriction in the past had failed to restrict. That a year's acquaintance with the working out of the policy of effective restriction has not proved satisfactory to those people most closely in touch with the situation is evidenced by the introduction at this session of a similar resolution, or rather a bill to provide for the exclusion of orientals. The supporters of this resolution on race-track gambling take very much the same attitude as was taken by every hon. member from British Columbia on their special race 'problem, and when we find men of the physical and mental breadth of the hon. member for Victoria City advocating effective restriction in the case of orientals, in which an international question is involved, and opposing effective restriction in the matter of race-

Race-Track Bettin/j
track gambling we are led to exclaim, Oh, consistency, thou art a jewel!
I was also rather amused with the amiable address given by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret). His efforts were apparently directed to the reducing of the able argument of the mover of this motion (Mr. Good) to an absurdity and to accomplish this he travelled over a wide field ranging from silk socks to the Ten Commandments. He also introduced into this discussion the question of personal liberty. Without developing this idea at any length, I would like to make a few comments upon the relation of personal liberty to the welfare of the family, of the community, and of the nation. Only last evening with a few congenial friends I wended my way to the Arena, and there enjoyed a contest in skill, endurance and sportsmanship. No doubt, Mr. Speaker, every man of the twelve on the two opposing teams had very emphatic notions as to his personal rights and personal liberties, but I noticed in addition to the twelve men on the opposing teams, there were two other men whose business it seemed to be to teach every member of those two teams the fact that his personal liberty was subservient to that of the other members on the teams and also to the rules of the game.

speechtext: Would not that be an example of regulating the game and not prohibiting it?
