speechtext: I think it was a question of regulating, all right. If a man proceeded harmlessly to kick the puck with his skate he was promptly called back, or if he gave an opposing player the butt end of his stick, even in retaliation, he was promptly benched. Even that little piece of black rubber on the ice had apparently certain rights and precedence over the rights of the players. The player at all times had to give the right of precedence to Miss Puck, or be promptly called offside. My hon. friend has no doubt observed that in the operation of his automobile there are also certain restrictions upon personal liberty. There are certain conditions of traffic to which the driver of an automobile must conform; the rate of speed is limited to a certain mileage. The law says, "Thou shalt not drive on the wrong side of the street; thou shalt not pass a waiting street car." In the Ten Commandments, which I am glad to know my hon. friend makes the rule of his living, there is the prohibition "Thou shalt not kill" and there are other things which affect his personal liberty.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subtopic: RACE-TRACK BETTING MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: Is there in the Ten Commandments the prohibition "Thou shalt not bet"?

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subtopic: RACE-TRACK BETTING MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
No, but there is this admonition "Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's goods." To argue for personal liberty is to argue for something that sounds ideal, but when personal liberty is gained at the sacrifice of family happiness, or community or national welfare, the person presenting the argument assumes a rather cheap position and the argument itself is scarcely worthy of any serious consideration. We are told in the Holy Writ "Whosoever will be chief among you let him be your servant." What is asked for in this resolution is that the law be made consistent, that the business of betting on race-tracks be made a crime as has already been done in the case of betting off racetracks ; that pari-mutuel machines be prohibited as book making and pool selling have been prohibited.
Why do we ask for this? I have heard some hon. members stress the fact that betting is permitted in England. I would like to point out that betting by pari-mutuel machines is prohibited on the tracks in Old England. In the year 1871 two men were convicted at Wolverhampton of trying to operate parimutuel machines. Those men were convicted and the law has ever since held good. Last year the question was raised there but was defeated in the House. Forty-five out of forty-eight states in the American union prohibit the use of the pari-mutuel machine and commercialized betting. I think we were told to-day that three states of the union had tried other forms of betting but had gone back to the pari-mutuel machine. I am not sure that at all times the majority is right, but when we find forty-five states following a certain course, when we find them prohibiting betting on race-tracks, and that there are only three states in this instance, I am inclined to think that the majority is right.
We ask for this resolution to become law because of the immoral influences of this business, as disclosed before the Commission of Inquiry in 1910 and the Rutherford Commission as well. On those occasions many examples were given to show that characters had been ruined, reputations shattered, homes destroyed, women's hearts broken, and little children robbed of their right to a happy childhood and a fighting chance in life. Furthermore, legalized betting on race-tracks is undesirable on economic grounds, because of the loss and confusion in business due to the failure of clerks and others in mercantile life

Race-Track Betting

to satisfactorily discharge their duties, their thoughts being far away on race-track gambling. I think it was mentioned by an hon. member here this afternoon that the Quebec Board of Trade had introduced a resolution opposing this practice. Manufacturers of British Columbia, and also the retail merchants of that province, I believe, have passed a similar resolution.
In the next place we are firmly opposed to legalized race-track gambling because it is a national scandal. Followers of the racetrack have been driven out of forty-five states of the union and now find their paradise for racing in Canada and Mexico. I remember reading years ago that negroes in the country to the south of us, in order to escape from the trials and sorrows that were their lot as slaves, were willing to risk pursuit by bloodhounds, willing to risk any peril, in order to escape from bondage. And when they made their dash for freedom to what haven did they flee. They came to Canada, the land of promise in the north, and by underground railway, by riding on ice floes as Eliza did in Uncle Tom's Cabin, and in many other ways, they sought to escape into the land of freedom and of purity, Canada. I am sorry, Sir, that when we think of some of the plague spots in Canada at the present time we cannot thrill with that same pride in our country that we ought to feel. To paraphrase Goldsmith :
111 fares the land, to hastening ills a prey,
Where vice accumulates and men decay.
Comparing the conditions in regard to this practice in 1917, under suppression, and in 1921 under restriction, I can only say that in this House, where the spoken -word is preserved for ages, I realize my personal responsibility to those whom I represent, and to those around me, and will take no chance that any spoken word or recorded vote of mine shall go otherwise than in support of this resolution.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subtopic: RACE-TRACK BETTING MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in listening to the speech just made by my hon. friend (Mr. Brethen), I was undecided as to whether I was sitting in the House of Commons or attending a revival camp meeting. We have heard speeches on this resolution which could well have been delivered from the pulpit. This question has been treated by hon. members of this House as if it were a religious matter, and not simply a legal question to be decided according to the ordinary rules which apply to questions of 
that character. Really, listening to the last speaker, one would never think it were possible for a member of the United Farmers of Ontario to have anything to do with horsebreeding or horse-racing. I would refer my hon. friend to the Canadian Sportsman and Live Stock Journal, established in 1870. If he looks at the issue of the date Monday January 29th, 1922, I am sure he will be surprised to see on the front page a picture of Canada's iron horse, Jack Canuck, owned by Mr. Morrison, the secretary of the U. F. O. This is-for us-not a matter of religion and it is not a matter of morality. It is a question of common sense, and it is from the standpoint of common sense that I wish to discuss the resolution introduced by my hon. friend for Brant (Mr. Good).
In discussing the merits of this resolution I do not wish in any way to criticize the hon. member. He holds most peculiar-most exceptional-views on certain subjects, but every man is entitled to his opinions and to his views. I respect his views and admire the courage with which he voices them in the House. I have heard, with great surprise, my good friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) telling us that he was going to support the resolution on the one hand; but, on the othpr hand, being a thorough Liberal, he did not intend in any way to impose his views on eastern Canada. How the hon. minister could take that stand is beyond my comprehension. The resolution has to be debated and voted upon as it reads, and not as it may be interpreted by the mild-mannered Minister of Agriculture. This resolution does away with the existing law concerning race betting. It applies to the whole of Canada- the province of Quebec, the Maritime provinces, the province of Ontario, as well as to every one of the western provinces. Unless the resolution be amended, if it be adopted in this House, and if a bill is passed along the same lines as the resolution itself, we will have in Canada a law prohibiting race betting from the Pacific ocean to the Atlantic coast. The hon. Minister of Agriculture says that he would not interfere with the freedom of the citizens of the province of Quebec, or with the freedom of the inhabitants of the province of Ontario or of the Maritime provinces. If the minister casts his vote in favour of the resolution unamended, he will force upon these provinces legislation which these provinces do not wish to have.
The resolution on its merits could be considered I submit, Mr Speaker, from a fourfold viewpoint. First, it could be considered from the constitutional viewpoint. Secondly,

is it in accordance with sound philosophical views? Thirdly, is it a resolution that could be supported without amendment according to the elementary rules of law? And fourthly, would it have the effect that my hon. friend for Brant wishes a law based on that resolution to have? From a constitutional viewpoint, has this House of Commons, or has the federal parliament, the power to prohibit betting in Canada? If we examine the British North America Act, section, 92, subsection 13, we will see that all laws concerning property and civil rights are to be enacted by the provinces and not by Canada. Under the provisions of that subsection, laws have been passed in the province of Quebec and are still in effect in that province. Then I would refer my hon. friend for Brant to the civil code of the province of Quebec, sections 1927 and 1928, which makes race betting absolutely legal. How can we, as members of the federal parliament, enact a law which would be outside of our competency as legislators? *

I think the hon. member would be in a better position to answer that question than I am myself. Let us examine what law is. What is a law? Why do we pass laws? Law is nothing but regulated freedom. Law is the enforcement of social order, so that man may live according to the customs or the modes accepted by the members of the community wherein he resides. Law is noth-

Race-Track Betting
ing but that. The law, as has been pointed out by speakers who have preceded me, prohibits murder, for instance; but a distinction has to be made, a distinction which is taught to us by sane philosophy. What is evil? There are two kinds of evil. There is evil which is essentially bad or, as we say in Latin, malum per se, evil fundamentally bad, and besides malum per se, there is malum per accidens, or evil accidentally. Malum per se needs no legislation. Malum per se is recognized throughout the world by every man who lives, and it is prevented by natural laws. Malum per accidens is sometimes prohibited, not by universal or natural law, but by written or local laws. I will give an example of fundamental evil. Murder is malum per se. We do not need any law to prohibit murder; natural law prohibits it, and it is forbidden throughout the world. Let me give an example now of malum per accidens.

speechtext: Certainly it does, and that explains why my hon. friend is here. I was going to give an example of malum per accidens. We have in this country laws which enact that a man has to go about the streets decently dressed. This is a local law, which does not exist in Patagonia, or in Africa. To go undressed is not malum per se; it is simply malum per accidens. What about betting? Would any member in this House say that betting is malum per se? If it is malum at all, it is malum per accidens, and who is going to give us the standard? Where are we going to find it? In my church it may be that betting is no evil at all. I will never admit that the church to which a good Scotchman like my respected neighbour goes can be the same church that I go to. If then betting is not an evil essentially, the question becomes a moral one, and moral questions are not for parliament, but for churches. It may be a sin to bet, according to certain religious tenets; but laws should be enacted in order to punish crimes, and religion should prevent sins. Let the religious bodies of this country so educate their members that they will not bet, if it pleases the preachers of these bodies so to do. But, Mr. Speaker, let not parliament become a pulpit for the rest of Canada.
I say that from the constitutional standpoint this resolution should not pass; from a philosophical standpoint it is not well founded,

and, in the third place, if you examine it from the strictly legal point of view it should be cast aside. This is nothing but another piece of uplift legislation. I am not surprised that my good friends the Progressives, and especially my good friend for Brant (Mr. Good), should be eager to introduce resolutions of this kind into the House. But if my hon. friend had sat in the House when the Hon. Mr. Rowell was here he would be sick and tired of that sort of legislation. This is not the first time in the history of the world that a parliament has tried to moralize people. Let my hon. friend for Brant remember what the first settlers in New England did when they came to the American continent. They passed the blue laws. And what was the result? So long as those restrictions on private liberty were imposed on the pioneers of New England material progress was retarded; and it was only when freedom blossomed, as freedom could blossom under the American sun, that New England became the most prosperous perhaps* of all the states in the great republic to the south of us. The Progressives have most peculiar ideas. Their main platform, one would say almost the whole of their platform, is the very broad plank of freedom of trade. Now, why should those hon. gentlemen who come here preach freedom of trade when they wish to deprive the people of Canada of every other kind of freedom? I am in theory a freetrader just as much as hon. gentlemen on the other side. But if 1 support the principle of freedom in the matter of trade I support the general principle of freedom in every direction, within the law. And I say that my hon. friends on the other side cannot support freedom of trade as the best possible arrangement between nation and nation if they deny, on the other hand, every kind and, species of freedom and liberty to the citizens of Canada.
As to betting, Mr. Speaker, our friends on the other side have also most peculiar ideas. When it comes to gambling and betting on the wheat crop they are prepared to put up their money. They asked us last year to pass legislation and institute a wheat board so that they might be sure to win on their bets and never lose. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) said that he would support the resolution because, if he voted against it, he would be false to the education he received as a young man. I may say to the hon. gentleman, with all due respect, that the education which a man receives is not limited to the years of his youth, and that he should be always open to improvement.
Now, let us examine this resolution-and it is my last point-from the practical stand-

point. Grant that the resolution is adopted; let us suppose that a bill is introduced and passed by parliament founded on the resolution, can that law be enforced? To ascertain whether it can be enforced or not, any hon. member who wishes to form a reasonable opinion should look around and see what has been the fate of similar laws passed in this country. Sanctimonious men have imposed on the majority of their fellowmen in the province of Ontario and elsewhere a law which is known as "Prohibition." How is it enforced? Can any man who sits in this House get up and sincerely say before this country that prohibition is enforced in Ontario? There is more liquor flowing in the province of Ontario than water in the summer time down the Montmorency falls.
Mr. GOOD; Perhaps that is not very much.

Quite a lot; and I would invite my hon. friend to come and see for himself. These laws, when it comes to putting them into operation, as has been demonstrated, are a premium on hypocrisy. If we . pass legislation of this kind we are simply creating a generation of hypocrites. Instead of having citizens who would openly and without fear go to horse-races and put their money on the horses that they think will win, you would have to-morrow a whole lot of people who would sneak behind doors to put out their money in the dark whereas now they put it out in the open daylight. What have you to-day as a result of prohibition in Ontario? You have a whole lot of hypocrites, who, when you meet them on the streets, you think are most respectable and law-abiding people. But if they are walking in a hurry, look at your watch, and if it happens to be around lunch time you can tell that they are hurrying along to have, before lunch, a little drink which they have hidden in the cellar. Laws of that kind are not good for the people. Instead of improving conditions socially they demoralize our population. Look to the south of us. My hon. friend who preceded me in the debate (Mr. Brethen) said that out of 48 states in the American union 45 had laws against betting. Has my hon. friend ever gone to a race meeting in the United States? Let him go where race meetings are held in that country and he will see that there is more betting done there than anywhere in Canada.. But not only would a law such as the resolution proposes put a premium on hypocrisy; it would put a premium on lawlessness. Instead of having race-tracks which are properly controlled and properly watched you would have race-tracks where a whole lot
of book-makers would hide around fences taking the people's money and robbing them, just as the bootleggers are prospering in Ontario and the United States, selling rotten liquor at exorbitant prices.
Now, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) said that he was in favour of this resolution because race-track gambling was a danger to the natural resources of Canada, and he quoted figures relative to the amount of money wagered at race-tracks. But my hon. friend has a most peculiar way of adding figures-maybe because he never went to a race meeting. He gives the figures as being what he terms exorbitant, but he forgets that the total wagered does not represent the actual money disbursed; that a man, for instance, may put down the same five dollars seven times in one afternoon-each time he wins he can take his money and bet it again.

Then another argument has been brought forward: we have been asked to vote in favour of this resolution in order to improve the type of our citizenship. I have no doubt that this argument is urged in entire good faith, but. is it not the fact that races can have, no effect whatsoever, on the character, standard, nature or calibre of our citizenship? When we go over to Connaught Park to see the races twice a year, whom do we find there? The best citizens in Canada. During the course of this debate we have had quoted some very sad cases, the saddest, perhaps, being that of the unfortunate young man whose honeymoon was interrupted because he went to the races. Well, really, if this young man was married to a wife who objected to her husband seeing a horse-race, I do not think that to-day he regrets very much being separated from her. But even admitting that all these cases were not at all overstated, after all they are only excep-
9 p m	cases, and there is a prin-
' ciple of law which is universally admitted, namely, that law is made to meet general cases, not exceptional. On account of this young man whose honeymoon was so sadly interrupted, on account of this grocer whose bills were so ill paid, on account of this poor unfortunate man in Toronto who gambled away his house, are we going to deny the rest of the people of Canada the pleasure of attending the races? I do not think the proposition is reasonable.
The fact that a resolution was passed by the Board of Trade of the city of Quebec is put forward as a strong argument in favour of this motion. I do not know much about the Board of Trade in the city of Quebec, and I know less about the resolution. Most probably that resolution was proposed by a few members who had lost money at the races the day before. But if my Progressive friends are so keen in using as an argument for their view a resolution passeed by the Board of Trade of the city of Quebec, I would ask them as a favour to also take into consideration the resolutions that the same Board of Trade has passed requesting the West to send us their wheat instead of sending it to American ports.
This session, Mr. Speaker, we have heard some most mournful speeches about conditions existing out West; also respecting Ontario conditions. If we wish to improve conditions in Canada, we have to give to the people some relief, we have got to give them a little enjoyment. As Victor Hugo said: Qui n'a trouve le repos dans un chant?- Who has not found entire repose in a song? Let us sing a bit and stop shedding tears. Let the people go to the races and hear the song of the horses as they go around the race-track. As those horses rush into the home stretch they give us the idea of friendly rivalry among the nations of the earth. And in that steeplechase of the nations, in that Derby of ideals, I will bet Canada straight on the nose every time.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that perhaps I am imposing 
on this House by undertaking to prolong the debate. It has been very interesting in the variety of views presented. I am unable, however, to take an extreme stand either way. I have not unlimited faith in making our people good by law. If I could feel that this resolution would do all that the mover of it thinks possible, I would take a good deal more pleasure in supporting it. From conviction I shall support the resolution, but I do not do so without a great deal of doubt as to its wisdom at this time. I have been connected with an exhibition association for more than twenty years and have diligently done the best I knew how to help build up that organization to where it is at present. I believe it will be very hard on that exhibition if we pass this resolution and the government enact legislation in accordance therewith. I am not without doubt as to the result. As I have said, I am not a very great believer in making people good by law.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY

speechtext:
We have had the parimutuel machines for several years; I do not know just how long. In my mind there is a doubt as to whether this betting could not be better handled through regulation of the parimutuels. I am not greatly interested in horseracing myself. I have seen the time when by moving a hundred feet or more I might have looked at some very interesting horseraces, but I was interested more in the other features of the fair, and attended to my business and let the horse-races go on. I have never bet, and I do not ever expect to bet on a horse-race, but I do know this, that in that thinly settled country people come from a long way to the fair who are very much interested in horse-racing. If we have betting without regulation, I believe that a certain amount of betting will go on, but I am a little fearful as to the effects on our fair if this resolution is passed and legislation is introduced to carry it into effect. Those fears may be overcome, I think, if all these people who are good enough to ask us to prohibit betting, which does bring a good many people to the fair, will turn in and help to make the fair a success without the horseracing. I believe that it could be done, but I find that the people who are perhaps the most religious and feel the need of this legislation most are the very ones who give us the least assistance in making the fair a success. I am not saying this to criticize them

Race-Track Betting
particularly, but as a matter of fact they are not interested in that line. I .have tried to be practical myself. Although I have not lent my assistance in any way to horse-racing -I have never been on the racing committee -I have tolerated it, knowing that we had to have the people there in order to make the fair a success, and I believe that that condition still exists in our district. I have to talk from my knowledge of the district where I live, although I believe that what I say is true of the exhibitions throughout Canada.
As I said before, I am willing to go the length of this resolution, but I want to impress on these people who are asking for our support that they are putting our exhibitions in danger. Perhaps some one will say that I am judging between the dollar and the welfare of the people, but an exhibition goes further than the money you take in. It means the welfare of the farming interest in that particular district where the fair is held. It is expected to mean that, and we try to have it mean that. So I would not like to be looked upon as putting the dollar before the welfare of the people and of the rising generation. With me it is a question of choosing between injury to the fair and benefit to the community where that fair is held. I shall have a certain amount of regret in voting for this resolution because of the fear I have of its result upon our association. I have helped to build up that association by long and diligent efforts, and if the government pass a law that would take away this support to our association, I would like to see them deal liberally with the association in the way of grants, and so forth, so that it might keep on its way doing the work for which it was intended, and a work that it can now do.
As a new force in politics this party has advocated more or less of moral reform, and as a member of that party I can go with our friends in voting for the resolution. We have asked for the abolition of gambling in our products, and we have asked that for a monetary reason. In that connection we have not talked of saving the men who speculate in our produce from hell fire and damnation; we have simply been thinking of the dollar we can save by preventing, speculating in our products. So we are not altogether free from advocating something that will bring in a dollar. When we look at human nature, we are all very much alike. We do not get very much apart, but it makes a difference who is affected. But I repeat, as this party has been working along the line of reform, I think it would perhaps be inconsistent if I were to
vote against this resolution, although I am quite convinced that it goes too far. On the other hand, there is undoubtedly a tendency among our young people to form spendthrift habits, and I am willing to help in any reasonable way to check the growth of irresponsibility and the spendthrift habits that our young people are forming.
I believe that if betting could be prevented it would have a good effect. I believe that if that were done it would steady our young people; but if horse-racing and betting are allowed to go on I think it will destroy and minimize the effect of stopping the use of the pari-mutuel machine and the practice of book-making, if the latter is actually in existence at the present time. From the experience that I have had I think that betting will continue if racing is allowed. If we could get not only the young people but the middle-aged persons interested in the live stock at exhibitions and induce them to concentrate on that feature it would have, in my opinion, a sobering effect. Unfortunately we have introduced another feature in connection with our fairs that the resolution does not deal with-a feature which I feel is more disturbing to the morals of the people than even horse-rading. I believe that today there is a greater interest taken in automobile races that are held in connection with our fairs than is manifested in the horseracing, and in my opinion that feature is going to be just as injurious in its effects. All these things tend to upset the steadiness of our people. I am a firm believer in the idea that an industrious people are going to be a happy and contented people. I do not want to make slaves of anybody, but it is a fact that too many of our young people today will not stick to a job either in the city or in the country. They are so bent on pleasure, so bent on running here and there in search of excitement, that they neglect and do not think very seriously about their business or the job they are trying to hold. I believe that if we are going in for prohibition of this kind we should prohibit all along the line. I cannot but think that automobile racing is upsetting people just as seriously as horse-racing does or has ever done. The experience at Edmonton fair last summer confirms me in that impression. On that occasion automobile races took place only during two days and yet the people thronged to witness those races in greater numbers than they did at any time during the rest of the fair. Let us be consistent. The reason I am willing to support this resolution is that I believe it is an effort to try and curb

Race-Track Betting
the irresponsibility of our young people throughout the country; to restrain them from forming habits that they cannot afford to cultivate; to check the extravagance that prevails; and to stimulate the practice of thrift-in a word to make them more useful citizens than they are at the present time.
I would be more strongly disposed to support the resolution if I had as much faith in reforming our people by legislation as most of the hon. gentlemen to my left seem to have. However, I do not agree with the sentiment which has been expressed by hon. gentlemen opposite that we can permit people to go without regulation in certain matters. I believe that the best kind of government we can have is a government that will, by its legislation, grant a liberty which does not infringe upon the rights of others. In a truly democratic country laws are enacted in the interest of the majority of the people. If that be not the case then I do not think there can be very much liberty in that country. We designate some members of the community as socialists. A socialist, I apprehend, wants the government to take care of him and see that he gets a share of everything good that is going. Socialists and anarchists are sometimes classed in the same category, but the anarchist is an entirely different sort of person. The anarchist wants liberty to do as he pleases regardless of the rights of others. He does not want the government to do anything for him and in reality does not want any government, at all. We must get somewhere between these two extremes, because a certain amount of regulation is necessary. Of course I do not want to over-estimate the amount of good that will result from regulation in this matter. I think we should attain the object aimed at if we did not build so much on what our exhibitions can do throughout Canada. These exhibitions undoubtedly have done a great work; they have had the effect of creating many better farmers than would otherwise have been the case. How are you going to make up for the number of people who pay for admission to see the horse-racing at our exhibitions? I would recommend the government to be liberal to these exhibitions so that they might operate and keep their business going even if they do lose a certain amount of patronage now derived from horseracing.

It* is all very well to quote Latin when you are in trouble, when you are likely to get deeper into trouble, and whenever the hon. member deals with ethics again, I advise him to use more Latin and use bad Latin that nobody can understand especially when dealing with people who understand ethics. His philosophy about murder and sudden death and all that is purely a creation of his own mind; there is no foundation ' for it in history, and it is about as reliable as his answer in regard to the question of natural selection asked by the hon. member sitting to my left.
I want to say that evil, whatever the hon. member says about it, is what the educated conscience of civilized man says is evil. That is what evil is, and it has no outward standard. It is relative to the state of your ethical education, and I leave it to your own judgment as to the point to which your ethical education has arrived. I am not setting up my standard as being perfect, but I do lay strong claim to my own view of what is ethical, and I have sufficient faith in my own ethical instinct to defend when necessary what I believe to be ethical, either in a personal or social sense. The hon. member is dealing with a subject that goes deeply into the convictions of many of us, and I would like to suggest that, when he deals with it again, he might, for our sakes and for the sake of everybody who takes these things seriously, adopt a more serious style of argument, knowing as he should know that he is dealing with convictions which are very much in the heart of all of us.
He said that all this must be left, not to a parliamentary, but to religious bodies; thai is their province; leave it to them; let them teach these things. I want to ask the hon. member, who are the religious people in Canada? In the first place, if this question has to be left to a religious body, I want to know what the religious body he belongs to has been doing all these years on this question. I do not know what religious body he belongs to,

Race-Track Betting
but if this question is to be left to a religious body, if it is responsible for the enlightment of the public conscience in this regard, I would like to know just where he has been receiving his education along those lines. My hon. friend says that this has to be left to the religious bodies of the land. Who are the religious people of Canada? Are not the religious people of Canada, all the people of Canada; and you can set the churches to the work-and I think the churches are not averse to the work; I do not think there is in this land an organized church that is averse to the work-of educating the people along ethical lines. We may sometimes differ and honestly differ as to what constitutes ethical advancement; but all the churches equally through all these years have been busily at work, at great sacrifice, educating the people along ethical lines.

That is a fundamental mistake that many speakers have made to-night. They think the churches of the land have worked a device to inveigle members on this side of the House to bring this resolution in to get over something that they themselves have not been working at. That is false. For a generation or more, the churches of this country have been doing their best to educate people along these lines, and education must have an issue; some day it must be crystallised into something. What is the use of education if, at some point, you cannot express it in the formula of the laws of the land, and, while we may be mistaken,-the vote to-night will prove to what extent we are mistaken-we believe that the process of education has been going on for a good number of years at such a rate that the time is amply ripe for a legislative expression of this education that has been going on.

maintopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
subtopic: RACE-TRACK BETTING MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in this debate; but it seems to me, from arguments advanced recently, that there has been a good deal of wandering from the evil which the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good), by his resolution, proposes to correct. Speaking as a member from the province of Ontario, I have not heard a great deal as to the evils of the pari-mutuel system or of the evil of betting on the race-track. What does exist as an evil in the minds, I think, of the majority of the urban population of Ontario, is the handbook evil, which is an acknowledged evil by anyone who has studied the question at all. The Attorney General of Ontario has pointed out, as was outlined to the House this evening in the remarks of the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), that this evil can be corrected or the enforcement of the law against the evil of handbook betting can be improved by restrictive legislation on the publishing of odds. It seems to me that in legislating further to restrict betting, when we have, against the greatest evil of betting, a law that is now not being properly enforced, we are taking on another piece of legislation which

Race-Track Betting
is going to make the enforcement of the law still more difficult.
I think hon. members in this House who are familiar with the American tracks at Saratoga will agree that there is just as much "whisper" betting, "word-of-mouth" betting and "sign" betting going on as there was in the days of open books. The legislation in the American states that have ruled against open betting has not been very well enforced, and we have' in Canada to-day more handbook betting than there is open betting under the pari-mutuel system. I do not think any hon. gentlemen who have studied the evil of handbooks will contradict me in the statement that not ten per cent of handbook offences are corrected by conviction. It is a known fact that in practically a large percentage of barber shops and poolrooms in Ontario, handbook bets are being taken, in spite of the fact that we have a law against handbooks.
I contend that the suggestion of the Minister of Justice is very much more in accord with correcting the evil of the system than is the resolution of the hon. member for Brant, for the reason that a day spent on a racetrack, aside altogether from the betting that may take place, is considered by most good citizens to be a day's outing. It is to be admitted that on any day's outing, whether it be at a circus, or a picnic, or a race-track, a man spends' a considerable amount of money, and that the figures compiled as to the amounts bet on the pari-mutuel system, do not represent the actual money spent in any way at all, because, as has been pointed out by previous speakers, money is bet and re-bet. If the hon. member for Brant would compile the amount of money spent at the thousand and one fairs, the midways that are held at the fairs, for which money no very great return is given to the citizens who are spending it, he would find that possibly the amount of money spent in this way for entertainment was just as great as the amount of money spent on the race-track. I contend that the betting of an odd day's sport by the citizens of this country is not an evil; but I agree with the hon. member for Brant that handbook betting which becomes a constant and every day source of gamble to the wage earners of this country, is one of the worst evils with which we have to contend. Therefore, I wish to record myself as being very much in favour of the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, at the suggestion of the Attorney General of Ontario, to frame laws to enforce the regulations against handbooks to the fullest possible extent. I think that if this parliament can legislate in that regard, leaving the
pari-mutuel system in existence for a time, and enforce that portion of the law, we shall be doing a greater good to the working men and the community in general than by putting restrictions on the pari-mutuel.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) tried to show that if money were wagered ten times it would be entirely dissipated. He stated that ten per cent of the rate was taken as a rake-off from the total bet under the systetn. That rate which is taken by the Ontario government is in the form of taxation, and if by his day's sport the citizen does contribute to the funds of the Ontario government or any other government he is only paying a tax on amusement such as is paid in the form of the stamp tax in moving picture theatres.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Brant is aware that there are two rake-offs, the rake-off by the racing association and that taken by the provincial government. The minister referred to the total rake-off, because he said that if the money were bet ten times it would all be dissipated. I did not assert that the total amount of money went to the provincial government; I said that only a percentage of the rake-off went to them, and that it was in the form of taxation which the person doing the betting on the track paid to the government for his day's sport. Under the handbook system, against which I speak, there is no rake-off either to the provincial government, in the form of taxation, or to anyone else. The Minister of Agriculture went on to state that this money was all dissipated. I know there has been a great deal of criticism as to the total budget of the provincial treasurer, and if the money is dissipated after it gets into his hands I cannot say. That may or may not be true. But I did not interpret the minister as taking a slam at the provincial treasurer when he said that the money that came off the racetracks was dissipated.
' I am not, Mr. Speaker, in accord with the suggestion of the Minister of Justice (Sir Lomer Gouin), who pointed out that if the resolution of the hon. member for Brant carried, and a law were enacted based upon it, that law should be a provincial option. I think that handbook betting is wrong. H this House decides that the pari-mutuel system is wrong, then, in the view of the people's representatives, the law is wrong. I do not think that this parliament should legislate for

speechtext:
I probably know as little, from personal experience, of the race-track gambling evil as any hon. member in this House. I attended one race in my life where money was being wagered, but I have had some experience of the results that accrue from racetrack gambling. In former days, in various cities on this continent, I have seen and come in personal contact with some of the results of this gambling to certain citizens of this and our neighbouring country, results that have not been discussed, as I have observed, to any great extent to-night. I speak for the women and children of race-track gamblers. Consult the records of one of the neighbouring cities in the country to the south of us for the past few years and you will find, as I have read, that a considerable number of divorces have been granted to women who complained that their husbands insisted on spending all of their money in trying to beat the race-track game. In my judgment these women and children are entitled to some consideration in a discussion of this kind. I believe that parliament is not going beyond its proper and consistent sphere of effort when it undertakes to deal with a question of such prime importance to many mothers, yes, and children throughout the length and breadth of Canada and the United States.
I have heard considerable argument to-day from hon. gentlemen on this side of the House and across the floor as to the right to let men gamble if they will. I know sufficient of human nature to be convinced that they will gamble. I am of opinion that if many of them did not get the opportunity to take a chance and bet their money on horse-races they would do so in shooting craps, playing poker, or something else. But I think I know

something, from personal contact, of the results of race-track gambling; and I know that the fever of this evil gets into the veins of men and causes untold suffering to those whom in many cases they are sworn to protect. One hon. gentleman a moment ago said that a race-track day is a day's outing for some men. That is right. I have no doubt that it is correct. The one afternoon I spent on the racetrack was for the purpose of an outing. But I wonder whether hon. gentlemen, in this House will concede that for very many thousands of mothers and children such a day is one of tragedy, when they find those who have promised to protect them squandering, just because the fever of gambling is in their veins, the money that should be supporting the wife and children in decency and comfort. I do not know enough about the general question, Mr. Speaker, to go into it at very great length. I do know, however, from personal experience that many of the results of racetrack gambling have been disastrous to women and children and many men too in the past. I shall certainly do what I can to remedy this evil by voting for this resolution.

The Minister of Justice also stated that there was nothing new in the case presented on this occasion, that it was just the same situation as existed in 1906 and 1910. That is partly true. This matter has been discussed in this House on several occasions. The principle involved is pretty much the same; the discussions that have taken place from time to time are pretty much the same, but since 1912 we have had a good deal of experience. We have had the experience that I quoted yesterday as to the effect which the 1912 legislation had upon racing associations and upon race-track gambling generally, and the effect that the order in council of 1917 had. In view of the additional information which we have gathered during these years and the experience we have had, we are in a better position now to know what is the proper thing to do than we were at that time.
As I said, I am Very pleased indeed to know that the government is likely to take action along the line suggested by the Hon. Mr. Raney in connection with the publication of betting odds and that sort of thing, all of which goes to encourage the hand-book evil.
Now with regard to the contention of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) that the provinces can put race-track gambling out of business by making the license fee high enough, I am inclined to doubt whether that is the case. I do not know, but I understand that the constitutionality of that procedure is in question.
So far as the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) is concerned, I found it almost impossible to take him seriously. I fancy he had a wink and a glint in his eye which betokened that he had to put up a good argument for a bad case and was making the best he could out of it. If I were to enter into a discussion of his philosophy it would take us rather far afield, but I do not think that any of us took him very seriously on this occasion. He entertained the House very pleasantly, and I am sure we are not sorry for that.

There has been extended to a number of people and organizations a special privilege to do what is defined under our criminal code as a crime. Do not let us confuse it with horse-racing, private betting, and a whole lot of other questions which have been dragged in during the course of this debate.
